chapters.name: Chapter 1: What AI can do for a nonprofit

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an AI assistant is, and what it is not
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain to a coworker or volunteer what an AI assistant can and cannot do for your organization.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of nonprofit tasks, you will identify which tasks an AI assistant can help with and which need a person or an official source, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
An AI assistant is a computer program you chat with in everyday words. You type a request, and it writes an answer in seconds. Well-known ones with free versions include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini.
For a nonprofit, it is good at first drafts: thank-you notes, newsletter articles, volunteer sign-up messages, meeting agendas, social media posts, and turning long reports into short summaries.
It is not a staff member, a lawyer, an accountant or a grant officer. It does not know your donors, your programs or your community, and it can be wrong even when it sounds sure. A person on your team always reviews and decides.
Words to know:
- AI: short for artificial intelligence: computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person, like writing or summarizing.
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or talking.
- First draft: a starting version that a person then checks and improves.
Try it now: List three pieces of writing your organization produces every month (for example a volunteer reminder, a donor thank-you and a newsletter). Circle the one that takes the most time. That is your first AI task.
You can now say what an AI assistant is, name three nonprofit tasks it can help with, and say why a person still reviews its work.

check.q: What is an AI assistant good at for a nonprofit?
options: First drafts like thank-you notes and newsletter articles
Making final decisions for your board
Giving legal advice you can rely on
check.why: AI is good at first drafts; a person on your team reviews and decides.

check.q: A volunteer says, "Let AI decide who gets this month's food boxes." What do you say?
options: Good idea; AI knows our community
No; AI can draft, but people on our team decide
Yes, but only for new families
check.why: AI does not know your community and can be wrong; your team decides.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Opening a free AI assistant
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Open a free AI assistant on a phone or computer and find where to type.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone or computer, you will open a free or approved AI assistant from its official website or app and sign out when you finish, without help.
You can use an AI assistant on a smartphone or any computer with internet, including an office computer or a church office laptop.
On a computer, open the web browser and type the address: chatgpt.com, copilot.microsoft.com or gemini.google.com. On a phone, install the official app from the app store, made by the real company (OpenAI, Microsoft or Google).
If your organization already uses Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, ask your administrator which AI tool is approved. A work account may have extra privacy protections that a personal account does not.
On a shared office computer, do not let the browser save your password, and sign out when you finish.
Step by step:
- Ask whether your organization has an approved AI tool.
- Computer: type the web address in the browser. Phone: install the official app.
- Find the message box near the bottom of the screen.
- On a shared computer, sign out and close the browser when you are done.
Words to know:
- Web browser: the program you use to visit websites, like Chrome, Edge or Safari.
- Administrator: the person who manages your organization's accounts and settings.
Try it now: Open one free AI assistant. Type: I volunteer at a nonprofit and I am learning to use AI. What are three ways you could help me this week? Read the answer.
You can now open a free AI assistant, find where to type, and check which tool your organization approves.

check.q: Where should you get an AI app on a phone?
options: From a link in a text from a stranger
From any app with a similar name
From the app store, made by the real company
check.why: Install the official app made by the real company, such as OpenAI, Microsoft or Google.

check.q: You finish using AI on the church office laptop. What do you do?
options: Leave it open for the next person
Save your password in the browser
Sign out and close the browser
check.why: On a shared computer, do not save your password, and sign out when you finish.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Asking for nonprofit writing in a clear prompt
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a three-part prompt that gets a useful nonprofit draft the first time.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real piece of nonprofit writing to do, you will write a three-part prompt that says what you need, the situation and the format, with placeholders instead of private details.
What you type is called a prompt. A good prompt has three parts: what you need, the situation (with no private details), and how you want the answer.
Example: "Write a short thank-you email to 25 volunteers who helped at our Saturday food drive. We served 140 families. Use a warm tone, under 120 words, and end with a date for the next drive: [date]."
A weak prompt like "thank you letter" makes the assistant guess, so the answer is generic. Tell it who will read it and what tone fits your organization: warm, formal, joyful or faith-based.
Step by step:
- Say what you need and who will read it.
- Add the situation: event, numbers, purpose. No names or private details.
- Say how you want it: length, tone, format.
- Use a placeholder like [date] for anything you will fill in yourself.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
- Tone: how writing sounds, such as warm, formal or cheerful.
- Placeholder: a marker like [date] that you replace yourself later.
Try it now: Take the task you circled in Lesson 1. Write a three-part prompt for it, using placeholders for names and dates, and send it. Save the answer.
You can now write a clear three-part prompt for a nonprofit writing task.

options: What you type to the AI assistant
check.why: What you type is called a prompt.

check.q: You need a flyer for a church dinner. Which prompt is best?
options: "Write a cheerful flyer for our church dinner on [date] at 6 pm, free for families, under 60 words."
check.why: A good prompt says what you need, the situation and the format.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Using AI safely and well

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Improving the draft
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use follow-up requests to turn a first draft into one that fits your organization.
This lesson builds toward: Given a first draft that does not fit, you will ask follow-up requests, one at a time, to change it, until it fits your organization's voice in no more than three tries.
The first answer is a draft. The assistant remembers the conversation, so you can ask it to change things one at a time.
Useful follow-ups: "Make it shorter." "Make it sound warmer." "Add one sentence about why volunteers matter to our mission." "Write it at a 6th-grade reading level." "Give me a version in Spanish."
Then make it yours. Add real names and details yourself, after you copy the text out of the AI tool, and read it as if you were the volunteer or donor receiving it.
Step by step:
- Read the first draft.
- Pick the one thing that most needs to change.
- Ask for that change.
- Repeat, then copy the text out and add real details yourself.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second request that builds on the answer you already got.
- Reading level: how easy text is to read; a lower grade level is easier.
Try it now: Take your saved draft from Lesson 3. Ask for two changes, one at a time. Then copy the best version into a document and add one personal detail yourself.
You can now improve an AI draft with clear follow-ups and finish it in your organization's own voice.

check.q: Why can you ask for changes one at a time?
options: The AI forgets everything after each message
Only one change is allowed per day
check.why: The assistant remembers the conversation, so you can ask for changes one at a time.

check.q: The draft is good but your readers are mostly Spanish speakers. What do you ask?
check.why: A follow-up can ask for a version in another language your community speaks.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking facts before you send
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find and check every fact in an AI draft before it goes to donors, volunteers or the public.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI draft with numbers, dates or claims, you will check every fact against your records or an official source, before it goes to donors, volunteers or the public.
AI assistants sometimes make things up: a wrong date, a statistic that does not exist, or a tax rule that is out of date. This is called a hallucination.
Always check numbers, dates, names, quotes, statistics, tax and legal statements, and anything about what a donation pays for. Check against your own records, the official source (often a .gov page), or the person who knows.
Never let AI invent impact numbers. If the draft says "we served 500 families" and your records say 140, use 140. Honest numbers keep donor trust.
Step by step:
- Highlight every number, date, name and claim in the draft.
- Check each one against your records or an official source.
- Fix or remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Ask a second person to read anything that goes to the public.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Impact number: a count of what your program achieved, like families served.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "Write two sentences about the need for food banks in my county." Highlight every number it gives. Try to find each one on an official site. Remove any you cannot confirm.
You can now spot facts in an AI draft and check them before sending.

check.q: What is a hallucination in AI?
options: Text that sounds true but is made up
check.why: AI sometimes makes up a date, statistic or rule; this is called a hallucination.

check.q: The draft says a $25 gift "feeds a family for a month." Your program never said that. What do you do?
options: Remove it or replace it with a fact from your own records
Ask AI if it is true
check.why: Never let AI invent what a donation pays for; check your own records.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Protecting donor, volunteer and client privacy
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI without putting private information about donors, volunteers or the people you serve into it.
This lesson builds toward: When you use AI for work about donors, volunteers or clients, you will keep private information out by using placeholders, sharing no names with gifts, addresses, case notes or health or immigration details.
People trust your organization with their information. Do not paste into an AI tool: donor names with gift amounts, home addresses, phone numbers, bank or card details, client case notes, health information, immigration status or children's details.
You can still get help. Describe the situation in general terms and use placeholders: "Write a thank-you to [donor name] for a gift of [amount] to our youth program." Fill in the real details after you copy the draft out.
Follow your organization's privacy policy, and ask a leader if you are unsure. When in doubt, leave it out.
Step by step:
- Before you send a prompt, read it for names and private details.
- Replace each one with a placeholder.
- Add real details only after you copy the draft out of the AI tool.
- Follow your organization's privacy policy.
Words to know:
- Private information: details that could identify a person or harm them if shared, like an address or a gift amount.
- Privacy policy: your organization's written rules for handling personal information.
Try it now: Final task: draft a thank-you note to the volunteers from a recent event. Use a three-part prompt with placeholders, ask for two improvements, check every fact against your records, and edit it to sound like your organization.
You can now use AI for real nonprofit writing while protecting the privacy of the people you serve.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Three-part prompt The prompt is vague, such as "thank-you note". The prompt says what you need, the situation and the format. It also names the reader and the tone that fits the organization. Two improvements Used the first draft as it was. Asked for two changes, one at a time, and the note got better. Can say what each change fixed. Facts checked A number, date or claim was used without checking. Every fact and date matches the organization's own records. Notes where each fact was checked. Privacy kept The prompt has a volunteer's or donor's private details. No private details in the prompt; placeholders used. Real names were added only after copying the draft out of the AI tool. Sounds like us The note sounds generic or not like the organization. Edited so it sounds warm and like the organization. A second person on the team read it and agreed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is safe to put in an AI prompt?
options: A donor's name and gift amount
"Thank [donor name] for a gift of [amount] to our youth program."
check.why: Placeholders let you get help without sharing private details.

check.q: You are not sure if a volunteer's story is too private to paste into AI. What do you do?
options: Share it on social media first
Leave it out and ask a leader
check.why: When in doubt, leave it out, and ask a leader.
